segments.source: Source A, written on the day of an event, says 40 carts arrived. Source B, copied 80 years later from an unknown account, says 90 carts arrived. Source C is an independent warehouse record from the same week and lists 42 carts.

When sources conflict, compare proximity to the event, independence, and whether a source has a reason or mechanism to record the specific fact. Agreement between independent relevant sources increases support but does not create absolute certainty.
Which account is better supported by the evidence given, and why?

1. A is contemporary and reports 40. 2. C is an independent operational record and reports 42, close to A. 3. B is much later and has an unknown chain of transmission. 4. The cluster near 40–42 is therefore better supported than 90.
An arrival count near 40–42 carts is better supported than 90.
Independent, relevant, well-positioned evidence usually deserves more weight than late repetition with unknown provenance.

1. A is contemporary and reports 40. 2. C is an independent operational record and reports 42, close to A. 3. B is much later and has an unknown chain of transmission. 4. The cluster near 40–42 is therefore better supported than 90. Cross-domain check: compare 14 with 8; 14≥8 is true.

Many explanations can be represented as condition-and-consequence rules. The logical form matters: necessary, sufficient, AND, and OR are not interchangeable.

Facts: Rain occurred; The river was already high; The warning siren worked; The gate was closed. Rules: If rain occurs AND the river is already high, flooding occurs. If flooding occurs, the riverside road closes. If the siren works, residents receive a warning.
Use the rules exactly as written. AND requires all listed conditions; OR requires at least one. A one-way implication cannot automatically be reversed.
Which consequences can be deduced by applying the rules exactly? Do not assume the converse of any rule.
1. Rain and high river satisfy both conditions of the first rule. 2. Infer flooding. 3. Flooding implies road closure. 4. The working siren independently implies a warning.
Flooding, road closure, and a warning can be deduced.
Causal reasoning becomes clearer when every link is stated and the direction of implication is respected.
Forward-chaining rule system over Boolean facts; apply implications until no new facts appear.

Facts: Rain occurred; The river was not high; The warning siren worked; The gate was closed. Rules: If rain occurs AND the river is already high, flooding occurs. If flooding occurs, the riverside road closes. If the siren works, residents receive a warning.
Use the rules exactly as written. AND requires all listed conditions; OR requires at least one. A one-way implication cannot automatically be reversed.
Which consequences can be deduced by applying the rules exactly? Do not assume the converse of any rule.

1. Rain is true but the high-river condition is false. 2. The AND rule for flooding therefore does not fire. 3. Without flooding, road closure is not inferred. 4. The siren rule still gives a warning.
A warning can be deduced, but flooding and road closure cannot be deduced.
